problems.title: Counting Nodes, Counting Leaves
problems.blurb: Two functions that look identical until you ask where the base case goes.
problems.statement:
Every problem in this gym walks a tree of Node objects. A node has a value and a list of children, left to right. A leaf is a node whose list is empty. The starter defines Node, plus build, which turns nested lists into nodes so trees are quick to write:

build(7)              a leaf holding 7
build([3, 12, 8])     a node with three leaf children
build([[3, 12], 8])   a node whose first child has children of its own

Write count_nodes(node), the number of nodes in the whole tree including the root, and count_leaves(node), the number of leaves.

They look nearly identical, and the difference between them is the lesson. count_nodes barely needs a base case: a leaf's loop over zero children adds nothing, so 1 + sum(...) already returns 1. count_leaves can't work that way, because an interior node must contribute nothing for itself — it needs an explicit leaf check.
hints: Trust the recursion: assume count_nodes already works on each child, then ask how this node's answer follows from theirs.
count_nodes(node) is 1 for the node itself plus count_nodes(child) summed over node.children. A leaf has no children, so that same line returns 1 without any special case.
count_leaves needs the explicit base case: if node.is_leaf(), return 1. Otherwise return the sum over the children with no + 1, because an interior node is not a leaf.

problems.title: How Deep It Goes, and What It Holds
problems.blurb: max() over the children is a MAX node in disguise -- and a leaf has no children.
problems.statement:
Write height(node): the number of edges on the longest path from node down to a leaf. A leaf has height 0.

Then write max_leaf(node): the largest value held by any leaf in the tree.

Both come down to max(...) over the children, which is a MAX node from minimax in disguise. Both also need a real base case, because max() of an empty sequence raises ValueError — and a leaf has no children to take the maximum over.

One trap in max_leaf: some trees give interior nodes a value too, written (h, [children]). Later problems use that as a heuristic estimate. Here it must be ignored entirely — only leaves count. Leaves can also be negative, so a running maximum that starts at 0 is wrong.
hints: height: a leaf is 0. Anything else sits one edge above its tallest child, so it is 1 plus the largest child height.
Check node.is_leaf() before calling max(). max() over an empty generator raises ValueError, which is exactly what happens when a leaf falls through to the recursive case.

max_leaf never reads node.value on an interior node: return node.value at a leaf, and the max over max_leaf(child) everywhere else. If you keep a running best instead, start it at float('-inf'), never 0.

problems.title: Leaves, One at a Time
problems.blurb: A recursive generator -- the shape of legal_moves() and successors().
problems.statement:
Write iter_leaves(node) as a generator that yields the value of every leaf, left to right.

This is the shape of legal_moves() and successors() in the homework. Callers consume it lazily, and a search that stops early never pays for what it didn't ask for. So beyond the order, the tests check that calling iter_leaves returns a generator, and that asking for the first leaf does not walk the rest of the tree.

The recursive step is where this goes wrong. Calling iter_leaves(child) on a line by itself just creates a generator object and throws it away — nothing is yielded. You need yield from.
hints: Use yield, and never build and return a list. A function with yield anywhere in its body is a generator, even on paths that never reach it.
At a leaf, yield node.value. At an interior node, loop over the children and pass along everything each child's generator yields.
yield from iter_leaves(child) forwards every value the child produces. Without it, iter_leaves(child) creates a generator that nothing ever iterates, and your function yields nothing below the root.

problems.title: The Route to the Best Leaf
problems.blurb: Return where the answer is, not just what it is -- with ties going to the leftmost.
problems.statement:
Write path_to_max_leaf(node), returning the route from node down to its largest leaf as a list of child indices. In the tree below the largest leaf is 14, reached by taking child 2 and then child 0, so the answer is [2, 0]. A leaf is already where it needs to be, so its path is [].

*
├── [0] *
│   ├── [0] 3
│   ├── [1] 12
│   └── [2] 8
├── [1] *
│   ├── [0] 2
│   ├── [1] 4
│   └── [2] 6
└── [2] *
    ├── [0] 14
    ├── [1] 5
    └── [2] 2

When several leaves share the largest value, return the path to the leftmost one.

This is the move half of get_best_move. The value alone is easy; the work is carrying the choice back up alongside it, and breaking ties the way the homework does — only a strictly better value replaces the current best, so the first one found wins.
hints: Write a helper that returns two things for any subtree: its best leaf value and the path to that leaf. The public function returns only the path.
At an interior node, loop with enumerate so you know each child's index. When child i reports (value, path), the path from here is [i] + path.
Replace your best only when value > best -- strictly. With >=, a later tie overwrites the earlier one and you return the rightmost path instead.

problems.title: Where a Depth Limit Stops
problems.blurb: Count the nodes a depth-limited search evaluates: get_best_move's leaf count, unpruned.
problems.statement:
A depth-limited search never looks more than limit moves ahead. It stops at a node for one of two reasons: the limit is used up, or the node is a real leaf with nowhere further to go. Every node where it stops is evaluated once.

Write count_frontier(node, limit), the number of nodes where that search stops. The root is at depth 0, so a limit of 0 stops at the root and the answer is 1. Nodes below a stopping point are never reached and don't count.

*
├── [0] *
│   ├── [0] 1
│   └── [1] 2
├── [1] *
│   ├── [0] 3
│   └── [1] *
│       ├── [0] 4
│       └── [1] 5
└── [2] 6

For this tree a limit of 1 stops at the root's three children. A limit of 2 stops at five nodes: the leaves 1, 2 and 3; the interior node [1][1], cut off by the limit; and the leaf 6, which the search reached early.

This number is the leaves count from the homework with pruning switched off. On the empty 3×3 dominoes board, get_best_move(True, 1) reports 6: six vertical moves, each child evaluated once.
problems.examples:
>>> tree = build([[1, 2], [3, [4, 5]], 6])
>>> count_frontier(tree, 0)
1
>>> count_frontier(tree, 1)
3
>>> count_frontier(tree, 2)
5
>>> count_frontier(tree, 10)
6
hints: Think of limit as moves remaining. Every step down a level uses one, so the recursive call passes limit - 1.
Check the two stopping conditions first: limit == 0, or node.is_leaf(). Either way this node gets evaluated, so return 1.
Otherwise the node itself is not evaluated: return the sum of count_frontier(child, limit - 1) over its children. Adding 1 for the interior node as well is the most common wrong answer here.

problems.title: Whose Turn Is It at This Level?
problems.blurb: The value of a game tree when both sides play perfectly, and the one-word flip that makes it work.
problems.statement:
In a game tree the levels alternate between two players. MAX picks the child with the largest value, MIN the smallest, and every leaf holds a score from MAX's point of view. The minimax value of a node is what it's worth when both sides play perfectly from there.

Write minimax(node, maximizing). When maximizing is True the node belongs to MAX, and its children belong to MIN.

MAX
├── [0] MIN
│   ├── [0] 3
│   ├── [1] 12
│   └── [2] 8
├── [1] MIN
│   ├── [0] 2
│   ├── [1] 4
│   └── [2] 6
└── [2] MIN
    ├── [0] 14
    ├── [1] 5
    └── [2] 2

This is figure 5.2 from the textbook. MIN's three nodes are worth 3, 2 and 2, so MAX at the root is worth 3.

The whole algorithm hangs on one flip: each recursive call passes not maximizing. Leave it out and every level belongs to the same player, and this tree comes out as 14.
problems.examples:
>>> tree = build([[3, 12, 8], [2, 4, 6], [14, 5, 2]])
>>> minimax(tree, True)
3
>>> minimax(tree, False)
6
>>> minimax(build(5), True)
5
hints: At a leaf, return node.value. It is already a score, whoever is to move.
At an interior node, compute minimax(child, not maximizing) for every child, then take max() of them if maximizing, else min().
If figure 5.2 gives you 14 you forgot to flip, so every level is MAX. If it gives 2 with maximizing=True, the flip is happening but max and min are the wrong way round.

problems.title: The Best Move Changes With the Horizon
problems.blurb: Depth-limited minimax returning (move, value, leaves) -- get_best_move without the pruning.
problems.statement:
Real game trees are far too big to search to the bottom, so the search stops after limit moves and asks a heuristic how good that position looks. Here each interior node carries that estimate as its value, written (h, [children]).

Write minimax_decision(node, limit) for MAX at the root. It returns (move, value, leaves) — the same shape as get_best_move:

  • move — the index of the root child to play.
  • value — the minimax value of the root, where any node at depth limit is worth its value, and so is any leaf reached sooner.
  • leaves — how many nodes were evaluated that way.

Break ties toward the leftmost child. There is no pruning yet; that comes in the Alpha-Beta tracks.

MAX  h=0
├── [0] MIN  h=4
│   ├── [0] MAX  h=2
│   │   ├── [0] 7
│   │   └── [1] 1
│   └── [1] MAX  h=9
│       ├── [0] 3
│       └── [1] 8
├── [1] MIN  h=6
│   ├── [0] MAX  h=5
│   │   ├── [0] 2
│   │   └── [1] 6
│   └── [1] MAX  h=1
│       ├── [0] 9
│       └── [1] 9
└── [2] MIN  h=3
    └── [0] MAX  h=8
        ├── [0] 4
        └── [1] 5

Search this tree one move deep and the estimates say play child 1. Two moves deep, child 2. All the way down, child 0. A deeper search sees replies the shallow one couldn't, which is exactly why the limit matters — and why a search that's accidentally one ply too deep or too shallow returns a plausible-looking wrong move.
hints: Write a helper search(subtree, maximizing, depth) that returns (value, move, leaves). Stop when depth == 0 or the subtree is a leaf, and return (subtree.value, None, 1) -- that one line covers both real leaves and positions cut off by the limit.
Recurse with depth - 1 and not maximizing. Add every child's leaf count to your total, whether or not that child's value wins.
Keep a child's index only when its value is strictly better (> for MAX, < for MIN). The recursive calls' moves are thrown away; only the root's is returned, reordered to (move, value, leaves).

problems.title: Pruning You Can Actually See
problems.blurb: Figure 5.7 as one function. The tests watch which leaves you read, so a search that never prunes fails.
problems.statement:
Write alphabeta(node, alpha, beta, maximizing), returning the minimax value of node using alpha-beta pruning exactly as in figure 5.7. The top-level call passes float('-inf') and float('inf') for the window.

Getting the right number is not enough. A minimax that never prunes returns the same value, so the tests hand you instrumented nodes that record every leaf whose value you read, and they compare that set with the leaves figure 5.7 evaluates. Skip one it needs, or read one it would prune, and the test fails and tells you which.

The details that decide which leaves get read:

  • After each child, a MAX node raises alpha to its best value so far, and a MIN node lowers beta.
  • MAX stops looking at its children once v >= beta; MIN stops once v <= alpha. Those are non-strict: an equal value prunes too.
  • Read a leaf's value only when you evaluate it.
problems.examples:
>>> tree = build([[3, 12, 8], [2, 4, 6], [14, 5, 2]])
>>> alphabeta(tree, float('-inf'), float('inf'), True)
3
>>> alphabeta(tree, float('-inf'), float('inf'), False)
6
hints: Start from your minimax: same base case, same flip of maximizing. Then thread alpha and beta through every recursive call.
In the MAX branch: v = max(v, alphabeta(child, alpha, beta, False)), then alpha = max(alpha, v), then return v if v >= beta. The MIN branch mirrors it with min, beta, and v <= alpha.
If the value is right but the test says every leaf was read, the window never narrows -- usually a missing alpha/beta update, or updating a copy that the next child never sees.

problems.title: Counting What the Search Evaluated
problems.blurb: Return (value, leaves) through every early return -- the bookkeeping get_best_move needs.
problems.statement:
Write alphabeta_count(node) for MAX at the root. It returns (value, leaves): the minimax value, and how many leaves alpha-beta evaluated to find it.

This is the third number get_best_move reports, and it's the one that exposes a broken search. Value and move can both come out right while pruning silently does nothing; the leaf count cannot.

Every call returns a pair now, including the early return on a cut-off. A leaf is worth (node.value, 1). An interior node adds up the counts its children reported — and the children it never reached, because it returned early, contribute nothing. That is the saving.

Figure 5.2 evaluates 7 of its 9 leaves. A search that reports 9 isn't pruning; one that reports 1 or 0 isn't adding the children's counts up.
hints: Write max_value(subtree, alpha, beta) and min_value(subtree, alpha, beta) inside alphabeta_count, each returning (value, leaves).
At a leaf return (subtree.value, 1). In the loop, unpack the child's pair and do leaves += child_leaves before the cut-off check, so the early return carries the count of everything evaluated so far.
Make the top call max_value(node, float('-inf'), float('inf')) and return its pair unchanged.

problems.title: get_best_move on a Bare Tree
problems.blurb: Depth limit, heuristic, (move, value, leaves) -- the homework's search with the game stripped away.
problems.statement:
Write alphabeta_decision(node, limit): alpha-beta for MAX at the root, looking no further than limit moves ahead, returning (move, value, leaves). It is get_best_move exactly, with the dominoes board replaced by a tree so nothing but the search can go wrong:

  • Stopping. A node at depth limit, or a leaf reached sooner, is evaluated: its value is node.value, and it counts as one leaf.
  • The move is the index of the root child. Replace it only on a strictly better value, so ties go to the leftmost child.
  • Pruning is figure 5.7's: update alpha at MAX and beta at MIN after each child, cut off on >= and <=.
MAX  h=0
├── [0] MIN  h=4
│   ├── [0] MAX  h=2
│   │   ├── [0] 7
│   │   └── [1] 1
│   └── [1] MAX  h=9
│       ├── [0] 3
│       └── [1] 8
├── [1] MIN  h=6
│   ├── [0] MAX  h=5
│   │   ├── [0] 2
│   │   └── [1] 6
│   └── [1] MAX  h=1
│       ├── [0] 9
│       └── [1] 9
└── [2] MIN  h=3
    └── [0] MAX  h=8
        ├── [0] 4
        └── [1] 5

Alpha-beta must return the same move and value that plain minimax does at every limit — 1, then 2, then 0 on this tree — while evaluating fewer nodes. At limit 3 minimax evaluates 10; alpha-beta needs 8. The tests check all three numbers, and when yours differ they check whether you match a known mistake: no pruning, strict cut-offs, ties breaking rightward, or a limit off by one.
hints: Two nested helpers, max_value and min_value, each taking (subtree, alpha, beta, depth) and returning (value, move, leaves). Stop when depth == 0 or subtree.is_leaf() and return (subtree.value, None, 1).

In max_value's loop over enumerate(subtree.children): recurse into min_value with depth - 1, add the child's leaves, keep i as the move if the child's value is > the best, then alpha = max(alpha, value), then return early if value >= beta.
Call max_value(node, float('-inf'), float('inf'), limit) and reorder its (value, move, leaves) into (move, value, leaves). This is the exact structure your homework's get_best_move needs.

problems.title: Name the Leaves It Never Read
problems.blurb: Report what alpha-beta skipped -- which means telling two leaves with the same value apart.
problems.statement:
Write pruned_leaves(node): run alpha-beta from MAX at the root with no depth limit, and return the values of the leaves it never evaluated, in left-to-right order.

This is the question exams ask about figure 5.7, turned into code. For figure 5.2 the answer is [4, 6].

The catch is that leaf values repeat. In [[3, 5], [2, 3]] MIN node [1] stops at 2, so its second leaf is pruned — but that leaf holds 3, the same value as a leaf that was evaluated. Keep a set of evaluated values and you'll wrongly report nothing. Record the leaf objects themselves (or their id()) instead.
hints: Two passes. First run alpha-beta, recording each leaf at the moment you evaluate it. Then walk every leaf left to right and keep the ones you didn't record.
Create the record in pruned_leaves and have nested max_value / min_value helpers add to it -- the same closure pattern as get_best_move's evaluation function.
Record id(leaf), not leaf.value. Two different leaves can hold 3; only one of them may have been evaluated.

problems.title: Dominoes, One Square Longer
problems.blurb: The whole DominoesGame class again with 1x3 pieces -- every bound moves by one, and the search must not care.
problems.statement:
Same game as the homework, with longer pieces. Two players take turns placing 1×3 pieces on a grid of Booleans (True = filled). The vertical player always covers (row, col), (row + 1, col) and (row + 2, col); the horizontal player covers (row, col), (row, col + 1) and (row, col + 2). The last player able to move wins.

Write the whole class from the skeleton, method for method as in the homework:

  • __init__, get_board, and the top-level create_triominoes_game(rows, cols).
  • is_legal_move(row, col, vertical) — all three squares in bounds and empty.
  • legal_moves(vertical) — a generator of (row, col) in row-major order.
  • perform_move(row, col, vertical) — fills the squares in place and returns None.
  • game_over(vertical) — whether that player has no legal move.
  • copy() and successors(vertical) — the latter yields ((row, col), new_game) in row-major order and never touches the original.
  • get_best_move(vertical, limit) — alpha-beta returning (move, value, leaves), scoring a board as the caller's legal moves minus the opponent's.

Every trap from the homework is still here, and a couple got easier to fall into. The piece reaches two squares past its anchor, so a bounds check copied from dominoes is wrong; boards are often not square, so checking a column against the row count only passes on square boards. And the evaluation must stay with the vertical passed to get_best_move at every depth — score from whoever is to move instead and the numbers stay plausible while the answers go wrong.
problems.examples:
>>> g = create_triominoes_game(3, 3)
>>> g.is_legal_move(0, 0, True), g.is_legal_move(1, 0, True)
(True, False)
>>> list(g.legal_moves(False))
[(0, 0), (1, 0), (2, 0)]
>>> g.perform_move(0, 1, True)
>>> g.get_board()
[[False, True, False], [False, True, False], [False, True, False]]
>>> g.game_over(False)
True
>>> create_triominoes_game(3, 3).get_best_move(True, 1)
((0, 0), 2, 3)
>>> list(create_triominoes_game(2, 4).legal_moves(True))
[]
>>> create_triominoes_game(2, 4).get_best_move(False, 1)
((0, 0), 2, 4)
hints: Get is_legal_move right first and everything else leans on it. Build the list of the three squares the piece would cover, then check each one is inside the board and empty. Compare row indices against the number of rows and column indices against the number of columns.
legal_moves is two loops over every square with a yield. successors copies, performs the move on the copy, and yields ((row, col), copy). A shallow copy of the board shares rows, so copy each row.

get_best_move is your homework's, unchanged: nested max and min helpers, stop on depth == 0 or game_over(vert_flag), recurse on the successor with not vert_flag and depth - 1, add up leaves, keep the move only on a strictly better value. The evaluation closes over the original vertical.

problems.title: Last Stone Wins
problems.blurb: No vertical flag, and a score whose sign depends on whose turn it is when the pile runs out.
problems.statement:
A pile of stones sits between two players. On your turn you take between 1 and max_take stones, never more than remain, and whoever takes the last stone wins. So a player who faces an empty pile has already lost.

The starter gives you the game — game_over, legal_moves (smallest take first) and successors. Write get_best_move(self, limit): alpha-beta, structured exactly like the homework, returning (move, value, leaves) for the player about to move. What changes is the evaluation, which is from that player's point of view:

  • +1 — the pile is empty and it is the opponent's turn: you took the last stone.
  • -1 — the pile is empty and it is your turn: they did.
  • 0 — the depth limit arrived before the game ended.

There is no vertical flag to pass around, because both players have the same moves. Whose turn it is lives in your recursion — a MAX call is your turn, a MIN call is theirs — so the evaluation has to be told which one it's in. An empty pile is not simply bad.

Nodes where the search stops count as leaves as before, and ties go to the smallest take.
hints: Reuse the homework's shape: max_value(game, alpha, beta, depth) and min_value(...), each returning (value, move, leaves), stopping when depth == 0 or game.game_over().

The stopping case needs to know whose turn it is. In max_value an empty pile means you are to move with nothing to take, so it is -1; in min_value it means the opponent is stuck, so +1. A pile that still has stones is 0.
If a single stone with limit 1 gives you (1, -1, 1), your empty pile is scored as a loss in both helpers. Taking that stone empties the pile on the opponent's turn, which is a win.

problems.title: Dominoes Where Nobody Owns an Orientation
problems.blurb: Same board, same 1x2 piece -- but with no vertical/horizontal roles, the homework's evaluation goes to zero and get_best_move needs take-away's win/loss trick instead.
problems.statement:
Same board representation as the homework, same 1×2 piece, same rule that the last player able to move wins. The one rule that changes turns out to change everything else: there is no vertical player or horizontal player. Whoever's turn it is may place a domino either way, freely, every turn.

Write the class from scratch:

  • __init__, get_board, and create_free_dominoes_game(rows, cols).
  • is_legal_move(row, col, vertical) — identical bounds-and-empty check to the homework's, for whichever orientation is asked about.
  • legal_moves() — no vertical parameter this time. A generator of every legal (row, col, vertical) triple, in row-major order over (row, col), trying vertical before horizontal at each cell.
  • perform_move(row, col, vertical) — fills the board in place, returns None.
  • game_over() — also no parameter: there is only one set of legal moves on a given board, not one per player, so there is only one way to ask whether the game is over.
  • copy() and successors() — the latter yields ((row, col, vertical), new_game) in the same order as legal_moves().
  • get_best_move(limit) — also no vertical parameter, returning (move, value, leaves).

That last one is the actual problem. The homework's evaluation was len(my legal moves) - len(opponent's legal moves). Here, "my legal moves" and "the opponent's legal moves" are the exact same set — legal_moves() doesn't know or care who's asking — so that formula is len(x) - len(x), always 0, on every board, useless as a heuristic.

What still works is TakeAwayGame's trick: a player who faces game_over() on their own turn has already lost. Score a MAX node with no legal moves as -1, a MIN node with no legal moves as +1, and a node cut off by the depth limit (with moves still available) as 0 — exactly the three-way split TakeAwayGame.get_best_move used, now evaluated against a real board instead of a pile of stones.
problems.examples:
>>> g = create_free_dominoes_game(2, 2)
>>> list(g.legal_moves())
[(0, 0, True), (0, 0, False), (0, 1, True), (1, 0, False)]
>>> g.perform_move(0, 0, True)
>>> g.get_board()
[[True, False], [True, False]]
>>> g.game_over()
False
>>> create_free_dominoes_game(1, 1).game_over()
True
>>> create_free_dominoes_game(2, 2).get_best_move(1)
((0, 0, True), 0, 4)
>>> create_free_dominoes_game(2, 2).get_best_move(2)
((0, 0, True), -1, 4)
hints: Start from your homework's is_legal_move -- the bounds-and-empty check for one orientation doesn't change at all. legal_moves is the same double loop as before, just calling is_legal_move for both True and False at every cell instead of only one.
game_over() is next(self.legal_moves(), None) is None -- same shape as the homework, just with no argument to pass through, since there's only one legal_moves() now.

get_best_move is TakeAwayGame's max_value/min_value almost unchanged: the stopping condition is game.game_over() (not a pile of stones being empty), the terminal values are still -1 for MAX and +1 for MIN, and depth == 0 with the game still going is still 0. The board-specific work is entirely inside successors() -- get_best_move itself barely changes from TakeAwayGame's at all.

If your version scores using a move-count difference like the homework's, expect every value to come out 0 or very close to it -- that formula can't tell any two non-terminal boards apart here, since both sides always see identical legal_moves().

problems.title: Alpha-Beta on a Dictionary Tree
problems.blurb: The quiz 4 question: alpha-beta over nested dicts, counting evaluations.
problems.statement:
Implement alpha-beta pruning: an optimisation of minimax that carries two bounds — alpha, the best value the maximiser can guarantee, and beta, the best value the minimiser can guarantee — and skips branches that cannot affect the final decision.

def alphabeta(node, depth):

The search starts with alpha = -infinity and beta = +infinity and returns a two-element sequence (list or tuple) [value, num_evals]:

  • value — the minimax value of the node, identical to what plain minimax computes.
  • num_evals — how many terminal evaluations were performed. One happens every time the base case fires. Pruned subtrees are never evaluated, so this measures what the pruning saved, and it is checked exactly — your pruning has to match.

Tree format

The game tree is plain nested dictionaries. Every node has:

  • "type" — "max", "min" or "leaf".
  • "value" — a number, present on every node. On a leaf it is the exact utility; on an internal node it is the heuristic to use if the depth limit stops the search there.
  • "children" — a list of child nodes. Internal nodes only; leaves have no "children" key.

The algorithm, exactly

num_evals depends on following this precisely:

  • Base case — if depth == 0, the type is "leaf", or the node has no children (key missing or the list empty), that is one terminal evaluation and the value is node["value"].
  • MAX node — start at float('-inf'). Visit the children strictly left to right; for each, recurse with depth - 1 and the current alpha and beta, then value = max(value, child_value) and alpha = max(alpha, value). If alpha >= beta, stop — do not visit the remaining children.
  • MIN node — symmetric: start at float('inf'), use min, tighten beta, and stop on the same alpha >= beta.
  • num_evals for an internal node is the sum over the children actually visited.

A recursive helper search(node, depth, alpha, beta) returning [value, num_evals], called from alphabeta() with the infinite bounds, is the shape to aim for.

def minimax(node, depth):
    children = node.get("children")
    if depth == 0 or node["type"] == "leaf" or not children:
        return node["value"]
    scores = [minimax(c, depth - 1) for c in children]
    return max(scores) if node["type"] == "max" else min(scores)
